sections.teks: A recount text retells the series of events or experiences that happened to the participant in the past in chronological order. Social function: to retell past events or experiences — dari laporan perjalanan sampai biografi tokoh.

Recount adalah saudara narrative yang paling sering tertukar. Bedanya tegas: narrative punya complication-krisis-resolusi (cerita rekaan berkonflik), recount memaparkan urutan kejadian nyata/kronologis. Soal TKA menyukai penukaran ini — kuasai pembedanya dan pola soal urutan waktu.

Bayangkan recount sebagai buku harian perjalanan: tanggal dan kejadian tercatat urut apa adanya. Narrative sebaliknya seperti film drama: ada konflik yang memuncak lalu selesai. Buku harian tidak mencari krisis — ia mencatat urutan.

Sequence of events — rangkaian peristiwa secara kronologis.
Re-orientation — komentar pribadi penulis tentang peristiwa (penutup opsional).

Read the following text carefully!

Vanessa Nakate's journey as a climate activist began in January 2019, after she became deeply concerned about the unusually high temperatures in her home country, Uganda. Inspired by the global youth strikes, she decided to take action by protesting outside the gates of the Parliament in Kampala. For several months, she stood alone with her handmade signs, despite the skepticism of passersby. This period marked her transition from a quiet graduate into a determined activist, as she demanded that the government acknowledge the climate emergencies affecting Africa.

Following her solitary protests, Nakate founded the Rise Up Movement to amplify the voices of other African activists who were often ignored by international media. A pivotal moment in her career occurred in early 2020 when she was famously cropped out of a photo with white activists at the World Economic Forum in Davos. Rather than being discouraged, she used the incident to highlight the marginalization of African voices in the climate conversation. This event propelled her into the global spotlight, allowing her to speak more forcefully about the "Congo Rainforest" and the unfair reality that Africa suffers the most while emitting the least carbon.

As her influence grew, Nakate shifted some of her focus toward practical solutions through the Vash Green Schools Project. She began launching initiatives to install solar panels and eco-friendly cookstoves in schools across Uganda. By doing so, she successfully reduced the schools' dependence on firewood and improved the learning environment for thousands of students. She also started advocating for the education of girls, linking it directly to climate resilience, and began traveling to various international summits, including COP25 and COP26, to challenge world leaders.

By 2021, Nakate had solidified her status as a global icon with the publication of her memoir, A Bigger Picture. The book documented her transformation and her fight for an inclusive environmental movement. Today, she continues to lead the Rise Up Movement and collaborate with international organizations like UNICEF. From a lone protester in Kampala to a world-renowned leader, Vanessa Nakate has proven that persistence can spark a massive shift in how the world views environmental justice and the power of youth.

(adapted from https://www.unicef.org)

What triggered Vanessa Nakate to begin her journey as a climate activist in 2019?
opsi: Her plan to work for the United Nations in Kampala
Her interest in joining international fashion movements
Her goal to publish a memoir about her graduate studies
Her desire to win an award from the World Economic Forum
Her concern regarding the unusually high temperatures in Uganda

Informasi ini dapat ditemukan pada paragraf ke-1 ( Vanessa Nakate's journey as a climate activist began in January 2019, after she became deeply concerned about the unusually high temperatures in her home country, Uganda ). Jalur Cara Gemilang: Trigger = peristiwa penyebab di paragraf pembuka; cari kekhawatiran/fakta yang memulai aksi.

Read the following text carefully!

Archbishop Desmond Tutu was a towering figure in South African history, known globally for his role in ending apartheid and his subsequent dedication to environmental justice. Born in 1931, Tutu rose to prominence as a vocal opponent of racial segregation, winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984. However, in his later years, he became one of the first global religious leaders to identify climate change as one of the greatest moral challenges of our time, famously labeling it "the apartheid of our era."

Tutu argued that the destruction of the environment was a profound injustice that disproportionately affected the poor and marginalized. He used his moral authority to call for a "global boycott" of the fossil fuel industry, similar to the sanctions that helped topple the apartheid regime. He believed that the same collective international pressure used to fight racial injustice should be applied to companies responsible for carbon emissions, urging institutions to divest from coal, oil, and gas to protect the planet for future generations.

His environmental philosophy was rooted in the African concept of Ubuntu, which emphasizes the interconnectedness of all living beings. For Tutu, caring for the Earth was an essential part of caring for one another. He frequently participated in international climate campaigns, signing petitions and recording messages that urged world leaders to transition to renewable energy. He saw the climate crisis not just as a scientific or political issue, but as a deeply spiritual one that required a fundamental shift in how humans relate to nature.

Until his passing in 2021, Desmond Tutu remained a "moral compass" for the world. His legacy lives on through the Desmond and Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation, which continues to advocate for social and environmental justice. By linking the struggle for human rights with the struggle for a healthy planet, he provided a powerful framework for modern activism. His life serves as a reminder that the fight for a better world is a unified mission that encompasses both social equality and ecological preservation.

(adapted from https://www.tutu.org.za)

Known as the heart of the "Red Centre," the Outback offered a landscape that was as intimidating as it was mesmerizing. I started my trek at Alice Springs, carrying a heavy pack filled with essential supplies, including several liters of water and a satellite phone, as the vastness of the desert leaves no room for logistical errors.

The silence of the Outback was unlike anything I had ever experienced; it was a heavy, humming stillness that made me acutely aware of my own heartbeat.

I had to navigate through narrow gorges and dried-up creek beds, constantly checking my map to avoid losing the trail among the shifting sands. By nightfall, the desert transformed completely. The temperature plummeted to near freezing, forcing me to huddle in my thermal sleeping bag. Reflecting on the trek, I realized that the Outback is not just a place of extreme conditions, but a sanctuary that humbles the human spirit. While attending a lesson at the Green School in Bali, they learned about significant world leaders who had made a difference. This realization prompted them to take immediate action, and in that same year, they co-founded a grassroots movement called 'Bye Bye Plastic Bags' (BBPB).

In the following years, the sisters organized numerous activities to strengthen their cause. They started by organizing large-scale beach clean-ups and delivering educational workshops to local schools across the island. However, they soon realized that to achieve a permanent change, they needed to influence government policy. To get the attention of local authorities, they even went on a symbolic hunger strike. This persistent effort eventually led to a breakthrough when they secured a meeting with the Governor of Bali to discuss the plastic crisis.

A major milestone was reached in 2019, when the Balinese government officially implemented a ban on single-use plastic bags, straws, and styrofoam. This landmark victory was the culmination of six years of tireless campaigning and served as a model for other provinces in Indonesia. After achieving this success in their homeland, the sisters expanded their mission globally. They established 'Youthtopia,' an international platform designed to provide mentorship and tools for young people around the world who wanted to start their own environmental projects.

The impact of their work was recognized by major organizations such as the United Nations and Time Magazine, which named them among the most influential teenagers in the world. They traveled to various countries to speak at international forums and urged world leaders to adopt similar plastic bans. The Battle of Surabaya began as a series of escalating tensions between Indonesian nationalists and British forces following the end of World War II. After Indonesia proclaimed its independence in August 1945, British troops arrived in Surabaya in October to disarm Japanese forces and release prisoners of war. However, conflict erupted on October 30 after the British commander, Brigadier General A.W.S. Mallaby, was killed during a clash at the Red Bridge. This incident prompted the British to issue a harsh ultimatum, demanding that all Indonesians surrender their weapons by the morning of November 10, 1945.

In the early hours of November 10, the Indonesian people chose to ignore the ultimatum, sparking a massive military assault by the British. The attack started with a heavy aerial bombardment, followed by naval shelling and a coordinated ground invasion of the city. Despite being significantly outgunned, the Indonesian militias and civilians refused to retreat. They engaged in fierce street-to-street combat, using both modern weapons and traditional bamboo spears to defend their territory against the highly trained Allied forces.

During the height of the fighting, a charismatic leader named Sutomo, better known as Bung Tomo, played a crucial role in maintaining the morale of the fighters. Through his fiery and passionate radio broadcasts, he urged the people of Surabaya to fight until the last breath for their freedom. His famous slogan, "Merdeka atau Mati" (Freedom or Death), echoed throughout the city and united people from various ethnic and social backgrounds. This collective resistance turned the city into a battlefield that lasted for nearly three weeks, far longer than the British had initially anticipated.

Although the British eventually secured the city, the battle became a significant moral victory for the Indonesian National Revolution. The heavy casualties and the immense courage shown by the Indonesians drew international attention and forced the world to recognize the nation's struggle for sovereignty. Today, November 10 is commemorated annually as "Heroes' Day" or Hari Pahlawan in Bahasa Indonesia to honor the thousands of souls who fell during this historic confrontation. The battle stands as a lasting symbol of the unwavering determination of the Indonesian people to remain independent.
